title: ME06b: When Growth Becomes the Work
author: Richard Claydon
summary: This installment of a serialised leadership narrative follows Maya, a senior leader, as four direct reports each take a 90-day developmental stretch in one quadrant of the Praxis Q model. Jo externalises her tightly held delivery rhythm into a shared playbook, Anil moves from smoothing tension to naming strategic patterns, Priya steps out of performed modesty into visible leadership, and Kieran learns to convene before concluding. Maya's coaching works through pointed probing questions, a named stretch posture and one concrete deliverable each. The central claim is that development need not sit on top of delivery as extra effort but can be embedded in the work itself, producing ripples across the team. It closes with reflection prompts for readers and a hook into the next rule about calibrating for the level.
points: Development can live inside delivery when each leader gets one quadrant, one stretch, one concrete deliverable and one ripple within 90 days.
Leaders who become the system's rhythm or sense-maker can limit their team's learning, so releasing control into shared playbooks and patterns builds capacity.
Maya's coaching relies on sharp probing questions and plain naming of the problem rather than workshops or competency models.
Modesty without presence is a form of erasure, so visible ownership can be an act of service to others.
Convening people around stories, mistakes and uncertainty creates relational early-warning systems and trust that private expertise cannot.
quotes: Maya had learned something simple but radical: development didn’t have to sit on top of delivery as extra effort. It could live inside the work itself.
Jo herself had become the rhythm. Every hand-off ran through her, every deadline echoed her vigilance. Her team executed flawlessly, but learned little.
Comfort, Maya knew, is a lagging indicator. Strategic coherence doesn’t appear by accident. Someone has to hold the tension long enough for shape to form.
Maya saw it clearly: Priya’s growth edge wasn’t competence. It was presence.
Kieran was brilliant, private, efficient. His country ran like a diagram: numbers tight, reports clean. Yet no one came to him with hard dilemmas.
Others began sharing too: a director on managing grief after an outage, another on fearing to be the weak link. Kieran didn’t solve it. He held it.
Development was no longer abstract. It was embedded in the work. The system grew smarter not through mandates, but through shared practice.
